extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers, and policy readers interested in law, human rights, and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and explain the legal, philosophical, historical, and practical standards that define and limit freedom of speech and expression across international, regional, and domestic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of freedom of speech / expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of speech is a principle that supports the freedom of an individual or a community to articulate their opinions and ideas without fear of retaliation, censorship, or legal sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes the right to seek, receive, and impart information or ideas regardless of medium; the article notes the terms 'free speech', 'freedom of speech', and 'freedom of expression' are often used interchangeably but that 'freedom of expression' is broader in legal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Everyone shall have the right to hold opinions without interference" and "everyone shall have the right to freedom of expression; this right shall include freedom to seek, receive, and impart information and ideas of all kinds, regardless of frontiers, either orally, in writing or print, in the form of art, or through any other media of his choice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UDHR Article 19 is cited as the international human-rights foundation for freedom of expression; used as a baseline normative standard in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICCPR Article 19 — permissible restrictions ('special duties and responsibilities')
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) amends Article 19 by stating the exercise of these rights carries 'special duties and responsibilities' and may 'therefore be subject to certain restrictions' when necessary 'for respect of the rights or reputation of others' or 'for the protection of national security or public order (ordre public), or of public health or morals'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes that freedom of expression is not absolute under international law; restrictions must be justified as necessary for specified legitimate aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated common legal limitations to free speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Common limitations or boundaries to freedom of speech relate to libel, slander, obscenity, pornography, sedition, incitement, fighting words, hate speech, classified information, copyright violation, trade secrets, food labeling, non-disclosure agreements, the right to privacy, dignity, the right to be forgotten, public security, blasphemy and perjury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these categories as frequently regulated across jurisdictions; justification for restrictions often invokes harm, public order, reputation, or morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle (John Stuart Mill)
rubrics_metrics.description: The harm principle suggests that 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill's argument is used to justify limiting speech only when it causes clear harm; the article cites Mill as the basis for many liberal defences of free expression and as limiting permissible suppression to prevention of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offense principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'offense principle' describes restriction on forms of expression deemed offensive to society, considering factors such as extent, duration, motives of the speaker, and ease with which it could be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify some speech restrictions where speech is deeply offensive even if not directly harmful; contextual factors determine permissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations based on time, place, and manner apply to all speech, regardless of the view expressed; they are generally restrictions intended to balance other rights or a legitimate government interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prohibiting a noisy political demonstration at a politician's home at night to protect neighbors' quiet enjoyment; funeral protests governed by state law in the U.S.; an activity identical in content might be allowed at a different time or place (e.g., daytime, public forum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brandenburg test (U.S. standard for incitement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[T]he constitutional guarantees of free speech and free press do not allow a State to forbid or proscribe advocacy of the use of force or law violation except where such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to incite or cause such action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted in Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), this test narrowed prior standards (like 'clear and present danger') and makes political speech broadly protected in the U.S.; requires intent/direction toward imminent lawless action and likelihood of such action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary privilege includes no possible defamation claims, meaning Parliamentarians are free to speak up in the House without fear of legal action. This protection extends to written proceedings (questions, motions, amendments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural/legal exception within many parliamentary systems that protects legislative speech to promote debate and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of information as an extension of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of information extends freedom of speech where the medium is the internet and may also refer to the right to privacy in IT contexts; it concerns the ability to access web content without censorship or restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites FOI laws (e.g., Ontario's Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, Canada's Access to Information Act) as legal mechanisms to secure access to government records and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative right characterization of freedom of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of speech is usually seen as a negative right: the government is legally obliged to take no action against the speaker based on the speaker's views, but no one is obliged to help speakers publish their views or to listen to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes non-interference obligations from positive duties to facilitate speech; it explains limitations on expectations that government must provide a platform or audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict with other rights (privacy, fair trial, honor, reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of expression may be limited when conflicting with other rights (for example, the right to privacy and the honor and reputation of others); greater latitude is given when criticism of public figures is involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that courts balance these competing rights and that standards differ depending on whether the target is a public figure or private individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the press vs. freedom of speech — media ownership concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of the press does not necessarily enable freedom of speech; if those who control media suppress information or stifle diversity of voices, press freedom can constrain speech — summarized as 'Freedom of the press is guaranteed only to those who own one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judith Lichtenberg's critique: press freedom without plural ownership can limit the effective availability of diverse voices; economic power ('no money, no voice') can undermine expressive pluralism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content moderation and platform governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media platforms frequently use content moderation to filter or remove user-generated content that is deemed against their terms of service, even if that content is not illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article discusses platform policies, the Communications Decency Act (CDA) and Reno v. ACLU as landmark U.S. cases concerning internet regulation; platforms' private policies create de facto speech governance separate from state regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet censorship and digital-era restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: With the evolution of the digital age, new means of communication emerged and are subject to new restrictions; countries or organizations may use internet censorship to block undesirable or illegal material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include national firewalls, blocking of content by governments, and platform-based moderation; the internet is characterized as 'speech-enhancing' but also a site of novel regulatory challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and jurisdictional variance — freedom of speech is not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Some do not regard freedom of speech as absolute; most legal systems set limits, particularly when it conflicts with other rights and protections, and national laws and cultural contexts vary widely (e.g., blasphemy laws, restrictions in Saudi Arabia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides historical and comparative examples (e.g., France's literary freedoms, India's constitutional limits for national security/public order, Saudi Arabian press restrictions) to show cross-country differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity and the Miller test (examples from case law and literature censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscenity laws (e.g., bans on Lady Chatterley's Lover, Tropic of Cancer) have been central to free-speech disputes; U.S. obscenity jurisprudence developed the 'Miller test' to determine what is obscene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts historical bans and landmark court rulings that overturned such bans, showing how legal standards for obscenity affect what speech is permissible and how judicial tests evolve.
